name: Middle part / curtains / textured crop trends
lead: Curtains is a men's hairstyle with a long fringe parted down the middle (or sometimes the side) and falling to either side of the face, with shorter sides and back [1]. A textured crop is a related short cut with a choppy fringe brought forward over the forehead [2]. People use these cuts to change how the upper face reads: the fringe can cover or shorten a high forehead and add visual width or softness around the temples [2].

Barber and style guides pair the cuts with face shapes. Man of Many lists middle-part curtains for oval, round, square and triangle faces because the hair falls over the forehead, and a forward-styled textured crop for oval, round and square faces, where the blunt fringe adds width to a longer face [2]. Looksmaxxing forum users make similar arguments, treating hair as a way to offset a perceived weak point [3][4].

Curtains have a long history, from early twentieth-century British working-class youth styles to late-1980s revivals and, more recently, an association with K-pop groups [1]. No clinical studies have tested these cuts.

Textured crop: short, choppy forward fringe [2]

paras: Curtained hair has a long fringe parted in the middle or at the side, with short or shaved sides and back [1]. The late-1980s centre-parted version derived from the bowl cut [1]. A textured crop, sometimes called a French crop, keeps the sides short and styles a choppy, blunt-cut top forward over the forehead [2].
Man of Many notes that middle-part curtains need regular combing and styling product to hold their shape [2].

Man of Many recommends middle-part curtains for oval, round, square and triangle faces and says the parted hair falls like curtains and hides the forehead. It recommends the textured crop for oval, round and square faces, saying a blunt forward fringe adds width to an elongated face and texture softens it [2].

The same guide quotes barber Lino D'Adderio on blending a fade to build weight at the temple and forehead, and quotes Nick Hall advising stylists to move the hair down and forward rather than up when covering a large forehead [2]. These pairings are the opinions of grooming writers and barbers; no controlled study of them is cited.

The Baiyue of the first millennium BCE appear to have worn short curtained hair [1]. In early twentieth-century Britain a long-on-top undercut variant was worn by working-class youth and street gangs such as Glasgow's Neds, Manchester's Scuttlers and Birmingham's Peaky Blinders; Glasgow Neds reportedly used paraffin wax to hold it [1]. New wave and synthpop fans revived a centre-parted style in the late 1980s, and Brendan Fraser wore it in the 1990s [1].
More recently the style has been linked with K-pop members including those of BTS, Monsta X and NCT [1].

Threads on looksmax.org compare curtains, fringe and other cuts. One poster argued that fringe or curtains suit everyone, citing pop and K-pop stars, and that curtains suit narrow eye spacing or weak cheekbones while fringe suits a poor hairline or forehead [4]. Another user asked whether curtains improve apparent interpupillary distance by covering bone lateral to the eyes, or reduce it by adding head width [3]. Other threads ask how to get the hair to lift at the centre part [5].

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, hair is discussed as a low-cost way to adjust the apparent proportions of the upper face [3][4].

claims.claim: Curtains or fringe can mask a weak point such as a high forehead or poor hairline
claims.believers: Forum posters say curtains suit narrow eye spacing or weak cheekbones, while fringe suits a poor hairline or brow ridge [4].
claims.experts: Grooming guides make a comparable forehead-covering argument [2]; no studies have measured it.

claims.claim: Curtains change apparent eye spacing (IPD) by covering or adding head width
claims.believers: One user suspected curtains cover bone lateral to the eyes but worried they add head width and reduce apparent IPD [3].
claims.experts: No published studies have examined hair and perceived interpupillary distance.

claims.claim: Fringe styles are what make pop and K-pop idols attractive
claims.believers: A poster argued stars and anime characters usually have hair falling on the forehead because it is an easy fix [4].
claims.experts: Wikipedia records the K-pop association with curtains but no research on its effect [1].

card.summary: Middle parts, curtains and textured crops: trending cuts with a long history and no studies on their effect on attractiveness.

quick.overview:
Curtains are a long fringe parted in the middle, with shorter sides. Together with textured crops they are among the trending men's cuts discussed online.

History sources trace the look to early 20th century Britain and revivals since the 1980s; no studies test its effect on attractiveness.
quick.mechanism: Fans say the fringe frames the face and covers the forehead or sides of the head. This is a styling claim, not a studied mechanism.
quick.risks: No health risks are reported for the cuts themselves.

chain: Fringe falls over the forehead and temples
Forehead appears shorter and the face softer or wider
Facial proportions read as more balanced
angle.text: A middle-parted or forward-styled fringe changes how much forehead and temple show. Style guides describe it as a way to balance a high forehead or a long, narrow face, and forum users use it to adjust perceived eye spacing or head width [2][3].
